methods.name: _load_segments_raw
methods.doc:
Populate _load_segs from raw ELF PT_LOAD program headers.

Reads program headers directly to build the complete VA→file-offset table.
This is needed for binaries with multiple LOAD segments (e.g. Huawei PPC32
which has a separate rw- segment at a different va-to-file-offset than the
rx segment).  Must be called after _load_lief/_load_pyelf.

methods.name: _fill_text_from_pyelf
methods.doc: Set _text_va/_text_off/_text_size from .text section without touching PLT.

methods.name: _load_plt_from_dynsym_raw
methods.doc:
Fallback PLT loader for PPC32 GOT2 binaries where LIEF reports 0 JUMP_SLOT
relocations (e.g. vendor-specific relocation type 0x40000054 in Huawei bootloaders).

On PPC32 Linux with -mrelocatable / GOT2 ABI, dynamic symbols with non-zero
st_value and SHN_UNDEF (st_shndx == 0) are PLT stub VAs.  Parse the raw ELF
to recover them without relying on LIEF's relocation type table.

methods.name: _build_got2_resolver
methods.doc:
Build GOT2-VA → symbol name map for PPC32 GOT2 PIC binaries.

In this ABI each compilation unit sets r30 = LR + addis_hi<<16 + addi_lo
at function entry (PIC prologue).  Indirect calls are:
  lwz  rX, N(r30)   ; load ptr from GOT2
  mtctr rX
  bctrl

Strategy:
1. Build plt_va → name from self._plt (already populated).
2. Scan the .got2 section (or all non-text writable data): for each 4-byte
   entry whose value is in plt_va_to_name, record got2_entry_va → name.
3. At call-resolution time, compute got2_va = func_r30 + N and look up.
4. Pre-compute r30 for every function by scanning the PIC prologue.

methods.name: _build_got_offset_table
methods.doc:
Build _got_offset_to_name for GOT-indirect bctrl dispatch.

PPC32 EABI secure-PLT / got2 ABI calling convention:
  lwz  rX, N(r_got)   ; load function pointer from GOT
  mtctr rX
  bctrl               ; call via CTR

r_got = GOT_base + 0x8000 (so signed 16-bit offsets cover the entire GOT).
GOT_base = minimum address in self._plt (the .plt/.got.plt section start).

methods.name: _resolve_bctrl_name
methods.doc:
Resolve a bctrl indirect call to a PLT name.

Handles two ABI variants:
- Secure-PLT / single-GOT: uses _got_offset_to_name keyed by signed disp.
- GOT2 PIC (Huawei PPC32): uses _got2_va_to_name keyed by got2_va = r30 + disp.

Expected pattern (2 instructions before bctrl):
  prev2: lwz  rX, N(rGOT)   -- GOT load; N is signed disp
  prev1: mtctr rX            -- load CTR from rX

GCC PPC32 ABI also emits `crclr cr1eq` (or other CR insns) between
mtctr and bctrl as a varargs indicator; when prev1 is such an insn,
fall back to prev3=lwz / prev2=mtctr.

Returns empty string if pattern not recognized.

taint_tracker_ppc64.py: PowerPC 64-bit network-to-sink taint analysis.

Architecture: PPC64 big-endian and little-endian.
ABI: ELFv2 (modern OpenPOWER Linux, POWER8+) and ELFv1 (AIX, old Linux PPC64).
     Both share the same integer register model:
     r3-r10 args (8 integer regs), r3 return value,
     r14-r31 callee-saved, r0/r3-r12/lr caller-saved.
     r2 = TOC pointer (callee must preserve in both ABIs).
     No branch delay slots.

Prologue (ELFv2): mflr r0   [save LR]
                  stdu r1, -N(r1)   [extend frame + save old SP]
                  std  r0, 16(r1)   [save LR in caller's ABI slot]
Prologue (ELFv1): same frame setup; function descriptor in .opd handles GOT.
Return:           blr               [branch to link register]
Call:             bl  <target>      [direct call]
                  bctrl             [indirect call via CTR, used for PLT]

Sources: recv/recvfrom/read/fgets/gets/fread -- return value in r3.
Sinks  : system/execve/execl/execvp/popen/strcpy/sprintf/memcpy/strcat/snprintf.

Targets: IBM POWER (AIX big-endian), OpenPOWER/POWER8+ Linux little-endian,
         old Linux PPC64 big-endian ELFv1, older Apple G5 macOS (big-endian),
         some network equipment (Juniper MX/PTX with POWER processors).

taint_tracker_rh850.py: GHS CC-RH / IAR RH850 ABI taint tracker.

Extends V850TaintTracker with three additions that the V850 tracker lacks:

  1. from_bytes / scan_function — flat ROM support for ECU firmware dumps
     (V850TaintTracker requires a well-formed ELF; automotive RH850 ROMs
     frequently ship without ELF headers).

  2. double_is_32bit flag — GHS CC-RH / IAR RH850 default is double=32-bit
     (§2.7 of GHS-RE-REFERENCE.md). A 32-bit double occupies ONE arg register
     (R6 or R7 or R8 or R9), not a pair. V850TaintTracker models the GCC ABI
     where double=64-bit and occupies a register pair (R6:R7). Without this
     flag, callers with double arguments show wrong register consumption:
     what looks like "R7 is second half of a double" is actually an independent
     scalar argument.

  3. GHS old-style symbol normalisation — GHS MULTI uses GCC 2.9.x mangling:
     constructors are ``Foo__ct``, destructors ``Foo__dt``, vtables ``__vtbl``.
     V850TaintTracker's source/sink resolver does not strip Renesas assembler
     underscore prefixes or recognise __ct / __dt patterns, so GHS-compiled
     constructor calls appear as anonymous call sites and are not matched
     against sink tables.

ABI: GHS CC-RH / IAR RH850 (GHS-RE-REFERENCE.md §2.2-2.4)
  Arg registers:   R6, R7, R8, R9
  Return register: R10 (scalar / pointer 32-bit), R10:R11 (64-bit)
  Link register:   R31 = LP
  Stack pointer:   R3 = SP
  Caller-saved:    R1, R6-R19, LP
  Callee-saved:    R2, R4 (GP), R5 (TP), R20-R29, EP (R30)

double type note (§2.7):
  Default: double = 32 bits (IEC 60559 single). Set double_is_32bit=False
  if the firmware was compiled with --double=64 (uncommon in ECU targets).

Targets: Denso RH850/G3M, Bosch GS327, Renesas R-Car E2 (R-Car D3/M3/H3 ECU).

module_doc:
Forward labeled-taint tracker for RISC-V (RV32 and RV64).

This is the labeled-taint path for RISC-V. It complements the existing
binary-path trackers (taint_tracker_riscv32/64.py) with:
  - Labeled Taint(labels, bound) model
  - TaintState with copy/join/same_as lattice ops for CFG fixpoint analysis
  - TaintEngine: linear dispatch over an Insn stream
  - analyze_cfg() path via cfg_riscv.py + analysis_riscv.py

Usage (listing path):
    from ablation.analyzers.taint_tracker_riscv import TaintEngine, Width
    from ablation.analyzers.insn_riscv import from_listing
    eng = TaintEngine(Width.RV64)
    eng.taint_register("a0", "user")
    findings = eng.run(from_listing(text))

Usage (CFG fixpoint):
    from ablation.analyzers.analysis_riscv import analyze_cfg
    from ablation.analyzers.taint_tracker_riscv import TaintState, Width
    init = TaintState(Width.RV64); init.taint_reg("a0", "user")
    result = analyze_cfg(insns, Width.RV64, initial=init)

Sources: recv/recvfrom/read/fgets/gets/fread
Sinks:   system/execve/strcpy/sprintf/memcpy/popen

ABI: psABI integer calling convention (a0-a7 args, a0/a1 return, s0-s11 callee-saved).

classes.name: Taint
classes.doc:
Labeled taint value.

``labels`` is the set of taint sources. ``bound`` is the maximum
attacker-controlled contribution to the value: after ``andi t, x, 0xff``
it is 0xff; after ``add p, base, t`` with a clean ``base`` still 0xff.
Any amplifying operation with no computable limit resets ``bound`` to None.

methods.name: join
methods.doc:
Least upper bound for a control-flow merge.

Labels: union. Bounds: max (clean side contributes 0); with ``widen``
a bound that differs between the two sides becomes None so loops that
grow a bounded value converge. Constants and frame_ptrs survive only
when both sides agree.

classes.name: TaintEngine
classes.doc:
Forward labeled-taint tracker over a linear :class:`Insn` stream.

Seed with ``taint_register(r, label)`` then call ``run(insns)``.
Findings accumulate in ``self.findings``; unknown mnemonics in ``self.unknown``.

taint_tracker_riscv32.py: RISC-V 32-bit network-to-sink taint analysis.

Architecture: RV32I / RV32GC (with optional RVC compressed instructions).
ABI: RISC-V Linux ilp32 / ilp32d calling convention:
     a0-a7 (x10-x17) argument registers (8 integer args), a0 (x10) return value.
     Caller-saved: ra (x1), t0-t6 (x5-x7, x28-x31), a0-a7 (x10-x17).
     Callee-saved: s0/fp-s11 (x8-x9, x18-x27), sp (x2), gp (x3), tp (x4).
     No branch delay slots.

Prologue: addi sp, sp, -N   [allocate stack frame]
          sw   ra, N-4(sp)  [save return address]
Return:   ret               [= jalr zero, 0(ra)]
          c.jr ra           [RVC compact return]
Call:     jal  ra, target   [direct call, PC-relative 21-bit offset]
          c.jal target      [RVC compact direct call, RV32C only]
          jalr ra, rs1, 0   [indirect call via register]
          c.jalr rs1        [RVC compact indirect call]

Sources: recv/recvfrom/read/fgets/gets/fread -- return value in a0.
Sinks  : system/execve/execl/execvp/popen/strcpy/sprintf/memcpy/strcat/snprintf.

Targets: SiFive / StarFive Linux SoCs, Allwinner D1, ESP32-C3 (RISC-V MCU),
         GD32VF103 (Gigadevice), Kendryte K210, OpenWrt RISC-V, PLCT RISC-V Linux,

taint_tracker_riscv64.py: RISC-V 64-bit network-to-sink taint analysis.

Architecture: RV64GC (RV64I + M + A + F + D + C compressed).
ABI: RISC-V Linux lp64 / lp64d calling convention:
     a0-a7 (x10-x17) argument registers (8 integer args), a0 (x10) return value.
     Caller-saved: ra (x1), t0-t6 (x5-x7, x28-x31), a0-a7 (x10-x17).
     Callee-saved: s0/fp-s11 (x8-x9, x18-x27), sp (x2), gp (x3), tp (x4).
     No branch delay slots.

Prologue: addi sp, sp, -N   [allocate stack frame]
          sd   ra, N-8(sp)  [save return address; sd = doubleword on RV64]
Return:   ret               [= jalr zero, 0(ra)]
          c.jr ra           [RVC compact return]
Call:     jal  ra, target   [direct call, PC-relative 21-bit offset]
          c.jal target      [RVC compact direct call -- RV32C only, not valid in RV64GC]
          jalr ra, rs1, 0   [indirect call via register]
          c.jalr rs1        [RVC compact indirect call]

RV64-specific additions over RV32:
  ld/sd (doubleword load/store), addiw (word add+sign-extend),
  addw/subw/mulw/divw/divuw/remw/remuw (32-bit operations sign-extended to 64),
  sllw/srlw/sraw, slliw/srliw/sraiw, c.ld/c.ldsp/c.sd/c.sdsp, c.addiw/c.addw/c.subw.

Sources: recv/recvfrom/read/fgets/gets/fread -- return value in a0.
Sinks  : system/execve/execl/execvp/popen/strcpy/sprintf/memcpy/strcat/snprintf.

Targets: StarFive VisionFive 2 (JH7110), SiFive HiFive Unmatched (FU740),
         Milk-V Pioneer (SG2042), SpacemiT K1 (X60), Canaan K510/K230,
         SOPHON BM1684 (64-bit RISC-V cores), OpenWrt RISC-V 64,
         PLCT RISC-V Linux servers, custom RV64GC embedded Linux.

taint_tracker_tricore.py: Infineon TriCore AURIX source-to-sink taint analysis.

Architecture: TriCore AURIX TC1.6x (little-endian).
ABI: Infineon TriCore EABI V2.9 / GHS EABI (GHS-RE-REFERENCE.md §1.2-1.3)
  Integer/scalar args: D[4]-D[7]  = d4, d5, d6, d7
  Pointer args:        A[4]-A[7]  = a4, a5, a6, a7
  Int return:          D[2]       = d2
  Ptr return:          A[2]       = a2
  Stack pointer:       A[10]      = sp
  Link register:       A[11]      = a11
  Caller-saved (lower context):   d0-d7, a2-a7, a11
  Callee-saved (upper context):   d8-d15, sp/a10, a12-a15, a0, a1

FCALL / FRET (GHS-RE-REFERENCE.md §1.7):
  Leaf functions use FCALL/FRET instead of CALL/RET.
  FCALL saves A[11] to stack only (no CSA). From taint perspective, same
  calling-convention effects as CALL: caller-saved regs are clobbered.

Sources: recv/recvfrom/read/fgets/gets/fread (return value in D[2] / A[2])
Sinks:   system/execve/execl/execvp/popen/strcpy/sprintf/snprintf/memcpy/strcat

Flat-binary usage (ECU ROM dumps):
    tracker = TriCoreTaintTracker.from_bytes(data, base_va=0x80000000)
    findings = tracker.scan_function(func_va, func_end_va, init_labels={'tainted'})

ELF usage:
    tracker = TriCoreTaintTracker.from_path('firmware.elf')
    findings = tracker.run()

Targets: Bosch ME17/MED17, Continental MG1, Waqas GEN3 ECU (AURIX TC1.6x).

taint_tracker_x86.py: Static intraprocedural x86-64 taint analysis.

Finds data-flow paths from network receive taint sources to dangerous sinks.
Implements the libdft taint policy (Andriesse, "Practical Binary Analysis", ch.11)
adapted for static analysis:

  XFER (mov/movsx/movzx):   dst_taint = src_taint
  ALU  (add/sub/and/or/xor/shl/shr/imul): dst_taint |= operand taints
  CLR  (xor rX,rX; sub rX,rX):  dst_taint = {}
  SPEC (lea):               dst_taint = union(base_reg, index_reg taints)
  CALL (source):            rax tainted; buffer arg tracked if on stack
  CALL (sink):              alert if relevant arg register is tainted
  CALL (other):             caller-saved regs cleared (rax/rcx/rdx/rsi/rdi/r8-r11)

Stack model: tracks rbp-relative and rsp-relative (with delta tracking) slots.

Usage:
    from ablation.analyzers.taint_tracker_x86 import TaintTracker, TaintFinding
    from ablation.analyzers.xref_graph import XRefGraph

    xg = XRefGraph.from_path(binary_path)
    xg.build()

    tracker = TaintTracker(binary_path, xref=xg)
    findings = tracker.run()
    for f in findings:
        print(f)

module_doc:
taint_tracker_x86_32.py: Static intraprocedural i386 taint analysis.

Finds data-flow paths from network receive taint sources to dangerous sinks.
Implements libdft taint policy adapted for i386 SysV / CDECL32:

  XFER  (mov/lea):            dst_taint = src_taint
  ALU   (add/sub/and/or/xor): dst_taint |= operand taints
  CLR   (xor r,r; mov r,0):  dst_taint = {}
  LOAD  (mov rd,[bp+N]):      dst_taint = stack_slot(bp+N)
  STORE (mov [bp+N],rs):      stack_slot(bp+N) = src_taint
  CALL  (source):             eax tainted; buffer length args tracked
  CALL  (sink):               alert if relevant pushed arg is tainted
  CALL  (other):              eax/ecx/edx cleared (CDECL caller-saved)

Stack model: tracks [ebp+N] frame slots (N<0 = locals, N>0 = incoming args)
and [esp+N] outgoing arg slots. esp delta is updated on push/pop/sub esp,N.

PLT resolution: handles both PIC (jmp *disp32(%ebx)) and non-PIC
(jmp *abs32) stubs via lief JUMP_SLOT relocations.

Architecture gaps filled vs x86-64 TaintTracker
------------------------------------------------
* CS_MODE_32 (i386) instead of CS_MODE_64
* CDECL32: args on stack, not in registers
* ebp-frame tracking (not rbp/rsp split)
* PIC thunk + GOT-relative string refs (ebx + disp32)
* PLT stubs differ: PIC variant uses jmp *disp(%ebx)

Confirmed targets (product.bin, asamba — Acronis True Image 2018 i386):
  product.bin: 56917 functions, system@plt=0x8081b00, execvp@plt=0x8084e10
  asamba:       7462 functions, system@plt=0x804b0d0, execv@plt=0x804b570

Usage
-----
    from ablation.analyzers.taint_tracker_x86_32 import X86_32TaintTracker

    tracker = X86_32TaintTracker.from_path('/path/to/elf32')
    for finding in tracker.run_interprocedural():
        print(finding)

module_doc:
Forward labeled-taint tracker for x86 / x86-64 instruction streams.

State
-----
* ``regs``       register family -> Taint. Sub-registers alias their family:
                 32-bit write in 64-bit mode zero-extends (SDM Vol.1 §3.4.1.1);
                 8/16-bit writes merge with the existing taint.
* ``mem``        (sp|bp family, disp) -> Taint: symbolic frame slots, rebased
                 across push/pop/sub rsp/leave, aliased on ``mov rbp, rsp``.
* ``ranges``     byte ranges (syscall input buffers, rep movs targets).
* ``consts``     known constants (mov r, imm; lea r,[rip+d]; zero idioms).
* ``frame_ptrs`` register -> (region, disp) for pointers derived from sp/bp.
* ``mem_ptrs``   slot -> pointer fact it holds (spilled pointer registers).
* ``ra_slots``   frame slots holding a return address.
* ``eq``         register equality class (full-width copies).

``bound`` on a Taint is the maximum attacker-controlled contribution to the
value: ``movzx eax, dl`` gives 0xff; ``lea rax,[rbx+rax*8]`` with clean rbx
gives 0xff*8; multiply by unknown or unbounded add resets it.

This tracker consumes instruction streams (from_listing / from_objdump /
from_capstone). For binary RE over ELF files use taint_tracker_x86.py.

Usage:
    from ablation.analyzers.taint_tracker_x86_labeled import TaintTracker, Mode, Abi, Policy
    from ablation.analyzers.insn_x86 import from_listing

    t = TaintTracker(Mode.X64)
    t.taint_register("rdi", "user")
    findings = t.run(from_listing(text))
    for f in findings:
        print(f)

module_doc:
tainted_string_tracker.py: upgrade SAC SNPRINTF_RODATA verdicts where format args are tainted.

Why this exists:
  SinkArgClassifier classifies `system(buf)` as SNPRINTF_RODATA when it finds that
  `buf` was written by `snprintf(buf, n, fmt, ...)` with a RODATA constant format.
  That classification is correct about the format — but it says nothing about the
  format arguments. The pattern:

      snprintf(cmd, sizeof(cmd), "%s %s", argv[1], argv[2]);
      system(cmd);

  ...produces SNPRINTF_RODATA even though cmd contains argv[1] and argv[2].

  TaintedStringTracker finds the snprintf call that produced each SNPRINTF_RODATA
  buffer, classifies the format arguments (rcx, r8, r9 for x86_64; stack for i386),
  and upgrades the verdict to ARG_PROPAGATED when any format arg is tainted.

  Gap ID: SAC-FORMAT-001

Usage:
    from ablation.analyzers.binary_context import BinaryContext
    from ablation.analyzers.sink_arg_classifier import SinkArgClassifier
    from ablation.analyzers.tainted_string_tracker import TaintedStringTracker

    ctx = BinaryContext.load_or_build('/path/to/binary')
    sac = SinkArgClassifier.from_context(ctx)
    results = sac.classify_all()

    tst = TaintedStringTracker.from_context(ctx)
    upgraded = tst.upgrade_snprintf_rodata(results)
    for u in upgraded:
        print(u)

module_doc:
TI COFF object file and AR archive parser.

Parses Texas Instruments COFF2 object files (.obj) and AR archives (.a) produced
by the TI Code Generation Tools (cl2000, c29clang, tiarmclang).  Extracts symbol
table entries including storage class, value, and section binding.

Supported formats:
    TI COFF2 object file   magic 0x00C2 at bytes 0-1
    Unix AR archive        magic '!<arch>\n' at bytes 0-7, members are COFF2

Target IDs (f_target_id at bytes 20-21 of COFF2 file header):
    0x0099  TMS320C6000
    0x009C  TMS320C5500
    0x009D  TMS320C2800  (C28x — the NNC F28x target)
    0x00A1  TMS320C5500+

Symbol storage classes (byte 16 of 18-byte symbol table entry):
    C_EXT    2   External definition (strong global)
    C_STAT   3   Static (local)
    C_EXTREF 5   External reference (undefined import)
    C_LABEL  6   Label
    C_UEXT   19  Tentative external definition — TI COFF equivalent of weak symbol
                 A C_UEXT symbol can be overridden by a C_EXT definition at link time.
                 cl2000 maps __attribute__((weak)) to this storage class.

Reference: SPRAAO8 — TI Common Object File Format (April 2009).

Usage::

    from ablation.analyzers.ti_coff_loader import TiCoffLoader

    loader = TiCoffLoader.from_path('/path/to/mod.a')
    for sym in loader.symbols():
        print(sym.name, sym.storage_class_name, hex(sym.value))

module_doc:
TI Neural Network Compiler (NNC) inference artifact scanner.

Detects TVM-generated `tvmgen_*` symbols in firmware compiled by the TI NNC
(ti_mcu_nnc, v2.x).  The NNC is built on Apache TVM and produces libraries for
TI MCU targets: F28P55x (C28x), MSPM0 (Cortex-M0+), CC2745/AM13x (Cortex-M33),
CC1352 (Cortex-M4), AM26x (Cortex-R5), F29H85x (C29x).

Supported binary formats:
    ELF (ARM Cortex-M33/M4/R5/M0+, C29x):  parsed via lief
    TI COFF2 / AR archive (C28x F28P55x):  parsed via TiCoffLoader
        cl2000 emits COFF, not ELF.  In TI COFF, the weak-symbol equivalent
        is storage class C_UEXT (19) = tentative external definition.

Security surface:
    NNC-generated headers declare normalization arrays as __attribute__((weak)):
        extern const float tvmgen_default_bias_data[]  __attribute__((weak));
        extern const float tvmgen_default_scale_data[] __attribute__((weak));
        extern const int32_t tvmgen_default_shift_data[] __attribute__((weak));
    Any object linked after mod.a that provides a strong symbol of the same name
    silently overrides the normalization parameters, changing the float->int8
    quantization boundary without any compile-time or run-time warning.
    In TI COFF, the same risk applies via C_UEXT (tentative external) symbols.

Finding classes:
    TINCC-001  HIGH    Weak normalization symbol override risk
    TINCC-002  MEDIUM  NPU async completion flag — ordering hazard
    TINCC-003  MEDIUM  Multi-model NPU contention (sequential enforcement required)
    TINCC-004  INFO    Skip-normalize mode active — manual normalization required

Usage::

    from ablation.analyzers.ti_nnc_scanner import TiNNCScanner

    scanner = TiNNCScanner.from_path('/path/to/firmware.elf')   # ARM ELF
    scanner = TiNNCScanner.from_path('/path/to/mod.a')          # C28x COFF AR
    result  = scanner.scan()
    print(TiNNCScanner.report(result))

module_doc:
v850_decoder.py: Renesas V850 variable-length instruction frame decoder.

V850 (NEC/Renesas V850E, V850E2, V850E2M, V850E3V5) is a RISC architecture
used in automotive ECUs, industrial controllers, and embedded systems.

Instruction width discriminant (bits[10:5] of first halfword = 6-bit opcode):
  op6 >= 32 (bit[10] of word set): 32-bit instruction
  op6 in (28, 29) -- PREPARE/DISPOSE: 32-bit (may extend to 48-bit)
  all other op6: 16-bit instruction

Key control-flow instructions:
  JARL disp22, reg2  [32-bit, op6=0x3E=62]
    reg2=r31 (lp): direct function call
    reg2=r0:       JR = unconditional relative branch
  JMP  [reg1]        [16-bit, op6=0x06=6]
    reg1=r31 (lp): return from function
    reg1=other:    indirect branch
  Bcond disp9        [16-bit, Format III: (hw0>>1)&7==3]
    conditional branch (bc, bnc, bz, bnz, bgt, blt, bge, ble, br, ...)

capstone 5.x and next branch have NO CS_ARCH_V850 support.
This module provides a pure-Python control-flow decoder.

ABI: V850 EABI (GCC default):
  r6-r9:  argument registers (a0-a3), caller-saved
  r10:    return value (also used as temp), caller-saved
  r11-r19: caller-saved temporaries
  r20-r29: callee-saved
  r30:    ep (element pointer), callee-saved
  r31:    lp (link pointer = return address)

Targets: Renesas RH850/G3M, RH850/G3MH (automotive ECU), V850E2R (industrial),
         V850E3V5 (dual-core ASIL-D), NEC V850E2 (embedded control).

Usage:
    from ablation.analyzers.v850_decoder import V850Decoder, V850Disasm

    dec = V850Decoder()
    frames = dec.decode_frames(data, base_addr=0)
    for f in frames:
        if f.is_call:
            print(f'call @ 0x{f.va:x} -> 0x{f.target:x}')

vendor_profile.py: load vendor-specific sink registrations and known-safe
exec patterns from YAML profiles in ablation/profiles/.

Usage:
    from ablation.analyzers.vendor_profile import VendorProfile
    from ablation.analyzers.sink_arg_classifier import SinkArgClassifier

    clf  = SinkArgClassifier.from_path('/path/to/binary')
    prof = VendorProfile.from_vendor('fortinet')
    prof.apply_to(clf)
    results = clf.classify_all()

Profile format (ablation/profiles/<vendor>.yaml):
    vendor: <name>
    sinks:
      - name: <symbol_name>       # PLT symbol to register as a sink
        arg_pos: <int>            # 0=rdi, 1=rsi, 2=rdx, ...
        note: <explanation>
    known_safe_exec_patterns:
      - id: <pattern_id>
        description: <why it is safe>
        fingerprint:
          unsetenv_strings: [...]  # env vars cleared immediately before execvp
        verdict: ELIMINATED
        seen_in: [...]
    known_sanitizers:
      - name: <symbol_name>
        charset: <regex-like description>
        note: <explanation>

The VendorProfile does NOT auto-eliminate findings — it pre-registers sinks
so the classifier can find them, and provides reference data for post-classification
annotation.  known_safe_exec_patterns are for documentation and future automation.

version_delta.py — Cross-version function tracking for ablation.

Tracks how a specific function
evolves across binary versions. Identifies homologs via a three-stage pipeline:

  Stage 1  Structural pre-filter   basic block count ±2, edge count ±30%
  Stage 2  Mnemonic 4-gram Jaccard sequence similarity, keeps top-10 candidates
  Stage 3  Semantic tiebreaker     SemanticSearcher when top-2 within 0.05

Patch localization via difflib.SequenceMatcher on normalized instruction lines
reveals the specific instructions that changed between versions.

Primary use case: track a specific function across firmware patch releases
to confirm CVE-2022-0778 / RADIUS overflow remediation.

no CFG load required. Results populate DeltaReport.anchor_results.

Args:
    era_only: if True and an anchor confirms the era, skip CFG analysis and
              homolog finding for that binary. DeltaReport.match will be None
              but DeltaReport.era_confirmed will be set. Use when you only need
              to know which era a binary belongs to, not the specific homolog VA.
    anchors:  override anchor library; defaults to ERA_DISCRIMINATOR_ANCHORS.

functions.name: structural_anchor_scan
functions.doc:
Scan binary bytes for known implementation-variant anchor sequences.

O(n) per anchor using masked pattern matching. A HIT definitively classifies
the implementation variant. A MISS is inconclusive — fall through to Jaccard.

The "patched vs unpatched" state is NOT visible from these anchors: all variants
represent the attr_list_add_impl function, which exists in both patched (MA
validation upstream) and unpatched binaries. Use VisorPlus/aimap for vuln state.

Args:

    anchors:  anchor library; defaults to ERA_DISCRIMINATOR_ANCHORS

Returns:

Classify a binary's parser implementation variant.

Layer 0 only — structural anchor scan.  Deterministic, <1ms per binary.
Returns variant='unknown' with confidence='unknown' on anchor miss; caller
should cascade to Layer 2 (mnemonic Jaccard) for novel/unrecognized builds.

Args:

Returns:

VtableDispatchScanner — finds call [reg+disp] dispatch sites in x86-64 ELF .text.

Determines which virtual function slots are actually dispatched (live) vs. never
called (dead). Covers all standard x86-64 indirect call encodings including
REX.B-extended registers (r8–r15) and disp8 / disp32 forms.

See docs/module-reference/vtable-x86-64.md for full documentation.

classes.name: VtableDispatchScanner
classes.doc:
Searches executable sections of an x86-64 ELF for vtable dispatch patterns.

Usage:
    scanner = VtableDispatchScanner.from_path('/path/to/lib.so')
    report  = scanner.scan({'method_a': 0x10, 'method_b': 0x4b0})

    # or pass a VtableMap from ELFVtableReconstructor
    report = scanner.scan(vtable_map)

    print(VtableDispatchScanner.report(report))

methods.name: _patterns_disp32
methods.doc:
Yield (prefix_bytes, modrm) for all call [reg+disp32] encodings.
ModRM = 10_010_rrr where 10=mod (disp32), 010=reg (/2=CALL), rrr=rm.
Skips rm=4 without SIB (handled by _patterns_sib_disp32).

methods.name: _patterns_disp8
methods.doc:
Yield (pattern, reg_name) for call [reg+disp8].
Only valid for 0 <= disp <= 127 (positive disp8).
ModRM = 01_010_rrr.

methods.name: _patterns_sib_disp32
methods.doc:
Yield patterns for call [base+index*scale+disp32] forms where rm=4 (SIB byte).
Covers common compiler-generated patterns: [r12+disp32] (REX.B, rm=4, SIB=0x24)
and [rsp+disp32] (rm=4, SIB=0x24).

Scan for dispatch sites for all slots in slot_map.

slot_map accepts:
  - dict of {name: slot_offset}
  - VtableMap (ELFVtableReconstructor) — uses live_slots() automatically
  - list / tuple of slot_offset integers

module_doc:
vtable_resolver.py — Static vtable reconstruction and BLR resolution for stripped ARM64.

Implements iResolveX-style indirect call resolution (Paper 23: "iResolveX: Resolving
Indirect Calls in Stripped Binaries via Learning-Augmented Static Reasoning"):
  Phase 1 — Candidate vtable extraction from .rodata (runs of ≥N code pointers)
  Phase 2 — Constructor vptr detection (ADRP+ADD+STR pattern → object type assignment)
  Phase 3 — BLR site detection (LDR vptr / LDR slot / BLR sequence)
  Phase 4 — Resolution: map each BLR@slot-k to target set from matching vtable regions

Binary hardcoded default: libwechatnetwork.so (WeChat 8.0.56 ARM64)
  .text   VA 0x000dd130  size 0x002de650
  .rodata VA 0x00032bf0  size 0x00064470

Primary target: BLR at ~0x112050 (fn 0x111f98) — passes &gILinkKey as x1 via unresolved
indirect call. Resolution goal: find vtable + slot for this dispatch.

functions.name: _canon
functions.doc: Canonicalize w-register names to x-register names.

module_doc:
wcode_parser.py: IBM W-Code (XLC internal IR) binary record parser.

W-Code is IBM XLC's proprietary intermediate representation used between the
front-end (xlCentry) and back-end (xlCcode) compilation stages. W-Code records
encode references to IBM compiler builtins — POWER-specific intrinsics, vector
operations, MASS math library calls, and IBM-internal control flow nodes.

This module provides:
  - WCodeRecord: a parsed W-Code binary builtin record
  - WCodeBuiltinCatalog: the builtin descriptor table extracted from xlCentry
  - WCodeParser: scanner for W-Code IR data (e.g., embedded in XLC .o files)

Format discovery:
  RE of xlCentry 16.1.1.3 ppc64le (path: exe/xlCentry in xlc.16.1.1_16.1.1.3-190404_ppc64el.deb)
  WcB_Lookup_Bif @ 0x11d88d00: parses binary W-Code records using lwbrx/lhbrx (byte-reversed
  loads), confirming the on-disk format is big-endian regardless of host endianness.

W-Code binary builtin record format (big-endian on disk):
  +0x00  uint32 BE   type_field_0    compared against WCB table entry +0x00
  +0x04  uint32 BE   type_field_1    compared against WCB table entry +0x08
  +0x08  uint16 BE   type_field_2    compared against WCB table entry (halfword)
  +0x0a  char[]      builtin_name    null-terminated; leading underscores stripped before lookup
  Total: 10 + len(name) + 1 bytes minimum

Short form (length <= 10): skip type-field comparison, name only.

W-Code builtin catalog in xlCentry 16.1.1.3:
  Table base:    TOC - 0x26720 = 0x12601960  (TOC = 0x12628080)
  Entry size:    0x28 bytes (40 bytes)
  Entry count:   2000+ entries
  Entry layout:
    +0x00  uint64 LE   field_0 (type ID or small integer)
    +0x08  uint64 LE   field_8 (parameter info or small integer)
    +0x10  uint64 LE   name_ptr (pointer to null-terminated name string in names pool)
    +0x18  uint32 LE   arch_mask (architecture compatibility ID; 0 = any)
    +0x1c  uint32 LE   pad
    +0x20  uint64 LE   field_20 (additional type info)
  Names pool:  0x11fe6010 (8-byte aligned null-terminated strings; names > 7 chars span blocks)

Hash table (for name lookup):
  Descriptor:  TOC + 0x416c0 = 0x126a96c0  (lhz capacity + ld bucket_array)
  Hash fn:     djb2 variant: h = h * 31 + c  (sldi r7,r0,5; subf r0,r0,r7; add r0,r0,r8)
  Bucket:      16-bit entry index into WCB table (0 = empty slot)
  Collision:   chain following via lhzx probes

Sample builtins:
  fltint, hscmplx, relax, rsqrt, rngchk, single, gcclongdouble, overflow,
  zerodivide, enable, imprecise, store, comment, linecont, reserve, preserve,
  cnv, par, pro, use, private, reduction, nooffset, aix, gnu, lute, large,
  smt, smt2, smt4, smt8, blend, balanced, fold, rrm, maf

Usage:
    from ablation.analyzers.wcode_parser import WCodeParser
    parser = WCodeParser('/path/to/xlCentry')
    catalog = parser.load_catalog()
    rec = WCodeParser.decode_record(b'\x00\x00\x00\x04\x00\x00\x00\x14\x00\x04fltint\x00')
    if rec:
        info = catalog.lookup(rec)
        print(f"{rec.name!r}: arch_mask={info.arch_mask if info else 'unknown'}")

classes.name: WCodeParser
classes.doc:
Parser for W-Code IR data streams.

W-Code files are IBM XLC's proprietary intermediate representation.
They are typically embedded in XLC-compiled .o files or generated as
standalone IR files by invoking xlc with IR output flags.

The on-disk format is big-endian (even on ppc64le hosts) as confirmed by
the lwbrx/lhbrx (byte-reversed load) instructions in WcB_Lookup_Bif.

methods.name: load_catalog
methods.doc: Load the WCB builtin catalog from the xlCentry binary.

methods.name: name_hash
methods.doc:
Compute the W-Code builtin name hash.

djb2 variant: h = h * 31 + c
Extracted from WcB_Name_Hash at 0x11d88e40 in xlCentry 16.1.1.3.
Loop: sldi r7, r0, 5; subf r0, r0, r7; add r0, r0, r8
  => r0 = r0 - (r0 << 5) + char = r0 * (1-32) + char = r0*(-31) + char
  => but with uint32 truncation (slwi r0, r0, 0): h = (h * 31 + c) & 0xFFFFFFFF

methods.doc:
Decode one W-Code binary builtin record from data at the given offset.

Returns None if the data at offset is not a valid record.

methods.name: scan
methods.doc:
Scan a byte stream for W-Code builtin record sequences.

W-Code IR files contain back-to-back records. This method is a
best-effort scanner; a proper file-header parser would need the
W-Code file magic and section layout (not yet fully reversed).

Returns a list of decoded records found in the stream.

methods.doc: Produce a human-readable summary of W-Code records.

module_doc:
window_analyzer.py: LLM-native bulk disassembly window for stripped ELF RE.

Motivation: per-instruction disassembly calls fragment LLM context across dozens of
round trips. This module dumps a configurable-size window (default 1536 bytes) centered
on any target VA, resolves PLT call targets and .rodata strings inline, and marks
function start heuristics (endbr64, CET stub patterns). One call = one annotated
chunk the LLM can pattern-match in a single pass.

Core workflow:
    wa = WindowAnalyzer.from_path('/path/to/binary')
    lines = wa.dump(va=0x41366, window=1536)
    # lines is a list of annotated instruction strings

    # Or dump to formatted text block:
    text = wa.dump_text(va=0x41366, window=1536)

Annotation format per instruction line:
    0x41366: call 0x3000          ; PLT -> target_func
    0x41371: lea  rdi, [rip+0x...]  ; "==diff==> %s:%d loading cli context fail"
    0x41290: endbr64               ; [FUNC_START]

The module reuses XRefGraph's PLT and string resolution when available.

classes.name: WindowAnalyzer
classes.doc:
Bulk window disassembler with inline PLT + string annotation.

Attributes:
    plt     : va -> symbol name for PLT stubs
    strings : va -> string content for .rodata references

methods.name: _load_xcoff
methods.doc:
Populate text bounds, plt, and strings from an XCOFF binary.

XCOFF .o files are relocatable: .text lives at vaddr=0 but at a
non-zero file offset.  Remap self.data to a VA-image so that
dump_text(va=0, ...) reads real .text bytes rather than the file header.

methods.name: _build_plt_ppc32_bss
methods.doc:
BSS PLT for PPC32/PPC64 SYSV ABI.

Stubs are written at load time by glibc, not stored in the ELF file.
Recover stub_va → symbol by correlating .rela.plt entry order with BL
targets in .text that land in the .plt VA range.  Stub size is always
8 bytes (2 words) for the glibc SYSV PPC32 BSS PLT; resolver_size is
inferred as (first_observed_consecutive_stub_va - plt_va).  The algorithm
is correct when stub index 0 is called from .text (the common case in
firmware with many imports).

methods.name: _build_plt_ppc64le_elfv2
methods.doc:
PLT stub resolver for ppc64le ELFv2 (OpenPOWER Linux, POWER8+).

ELFv2 places PLT stubs in .text, not in .plt (which is NOBITS at runtime).
Each stub is four instructions:
    std  r2, 0x18(r1)   ; save TOC
    ld   r12, OFF(r2)   ; load function pointer from GOT via TOC offset
    mtctr r12           ; move to CTR
    bctr                ; branch

TOC_BASE = .got_va + 0x8000 (ppc64le ELFv2 ABI convention).
Stubs are identified by the ld r12, OFF(r2) pattern; the stub VA is
the preceding std r2 instruction (which callers branch to).

methods.name: dump
methods.doc:
Disassemble starting from `va` (or a prologue before it) and return
annotated instruction strings.

Args:
    va        : center/start VA to disassemble from
    window    : bytes to disassemble (default 1536 = 1.5KB)
    align_back: bytes before va to include.  When > 0, automatically
                searches backward for an ENDBR64 / push-rbp prologue
                marker within `align_back` bytes and starts there,
                eliminating misaligned decode from raw-offset subtraction.
                Pass align_back=0 to disable alignment and start exactly at va.

The prologue search is arch-gated: x86_64 only (ENDBR64 → push rbp fallback).
Other architectures fall back to the plain va − align_back offset.

methods.name: dump_text
methods.doc: Return dump as a single formatted string block.

methods.name: find_func_starts
methods.doc: Return VAs of function start candidates in the window.

methods.name: calls_in_window
methods.doc:
Return (call_site_va, target_va, label) for all call/bl instructions in the window.
label is the PLT symbol name if known, else ''.

methods.name: align_to_func_start
methods.doc:
Search backward from `call_site_va` for a function prologue marker and
return its VA. Resolves the garbled-disassembly problem: backward scanning
from an arbitrary offset produces misaligned instruction decode.

Prologue search order (x86_64):
  1. ENDBR64 (f3 0f 1e fa) — CET control-flow integrity marker, always aligned
  2. push rbp (55) — classic frame pointer prologue

Returns `call_site_va - search_back` as a last-resort fallback (no alignment,
same as plain dump) so callers always get a valid start VA.

methods.name: dump_caller_context
methods.doc:
Convenience wrapper: disassemble the function containing `call_site_va`
and return the last `max_insns` instructions.

Delegates to dump(align_back=search_back) which now auto-aligns to the
nearest function prologue (ENDBR64 / push rbp) in the search window.

methods.name: dump_pseudo_c
methods.doc:
Produce simplified pseudo-C lines for each CALL instruction in the window.

Tracks register state (rdi/rsi/rdx/rcx/r8/r9 + rax) forward through
the annotated dump, then emits one pseudo-C line per CALL showing the
resolved argument values.

Single-basic-block only: no cross-BB tracking. Register state is
carried linearly; any branch resets uncertain registers to '?'.

Example output (from raw ASM):
    [0x41366] system("cmd_%s %s")   // ARG_REGS: rdi="cmd_%s %s"
    [0x413d2] snprintf(buf, 0x80, "%d: %s", local_10, arg_0)

Returns a list of pseudo-C strings, one per annotated CALL.

methods.doc: Return dump_pseudo_c() as a single newline-joined string.

methods.doc: Return the load VA (first PT_LOAD p_vaddr) for file-offset arithmetic.

Register state is tracked forward; each CALL line emits a call expression
with resolved argument names.  String annotations ('; "..."') from the dump
are used as the value for that register.

Format of input lines (from WindowAnalyzer.dump()):
    0x41366: lea  rdi, [rip+0x...]  ; "cmd_%s"
    0x4136d: call 0x3000            ; PLT -> system

module_doc:
windows_pool_taint_tracker.py — Pool allocation taint tracking for Windows kernel drivers.

Windows kernel memory allocation functions (ExAllocatePool*, ExAllocatePoolWithTag*)
return a pointer that subsequent code fills via RtlCopyMemory, memmove, memcpy, or
RtlMoveMemory. If the size argument to ExAllocatePool* is derived from user-mode
input (IoStackLocation->Parameters.DeviceIoControl.InputBufferLength or a
METHOD_NEITHER transfer) without proper bounds checking, an attacker can trigger
a pool buffer overflow by passing an oversized input.

This module:
  1. Finds ExAllocatePool* call sites via IAT resolution.
  2. Extracts the size argument (second argument in x64 fastcall).
  3. Finds copy-sink call sites: RtlCopyMemory, memmove, memcpy, RtlMoveMemory.
  4. Traces taint from the allocation size register to copy-sink size arguments
     within a configurable instruction window.
  5. Flags pairs where the allocation size and the copy size come from the same
     register / are unvalidated — these are candidate overflow paths.

Usage:
    from ablation.analyzers.windows_pool_taint_tracker import WindowsPoolTaintTracker

    tracker = WindowsPoolTaintTracker.from_path('driver.sys')
    findings = tracker.scan()
    print(WindowsPoolTaintTracker.report(findings))

Pool allocation taint tracker for Windows kernel PE binaries.

an intervening comparison — flagging candidate pool overflow paths.

module_doc:
WorkflowDocument — schema-validated stage output with deterministic routing.

Three gaps this closes:

1. SESSION.md is human-maintained flat markdown with no schema validation on stage
   outputs.  A finding_confirmation missing ``byte_proof`` is not caught until FORGE.

2. Stage routing is implicit in prose.  There is no machine-checkable transition rule
   between triage, sweep, profile, taint, confirmation, and registration.

3. Stage outputs are untyped and context-embedded.  State cannot be observed as a
   structured document or diffed across sessions.

Usage::

    doc = WorkflowDocument.for_re_session("cisco", "fmc_server")

    # validate before writing
    errors = doc.validate("triage", {...})
    if errors:
        raise ValueError(errors)

    # advance: validates, commits, returns next stage names
    next_stages = doc.advance({
        "binary_hash": "abc123", "arch": "arm64", "bits": 64,
        "section_count": 8, "string_count": 1200, "plt_count": 340,
    }, producer_id="session-42")
    # returns ["semantic_sweep"]

    # serialise to disk between sessions
    Path("session.json").write_text(doc.to_json())
    doc2 = WorkflowDocument.from_json(Path("session.json").read_text())

    # detect post-commit mutation
    doc.current().instance["arch"] = "x86_64"  # tampering
    assert doc.dirty_since_commit()

module_doc:
XCOFF32 AIX PPC32 BE function decompiler.

Why this exists
---------------
1. No open-source Python-native decompiler handles IBM AIX XCOFF32 binaries.
   Ghidra has partial XCOFF support but is banned from this toolkit; IDA/BN
   are commercial.  Neither understands the full AIX descriptor+TOC pattern.
2. ``Ppc476Decompiler.from_context()`` calls ``lief_parse(ctx.path)`` and
   reads the ELF ``.text`` section — this fails on XCOFF32 format, which LIEF
   does not fully expose as section data.  Every AIX binary (automountd,
   rlogind, ksh93, libc.a members) requires XCOFF32 parsing via xcoff_parser.
3. AIX XCOFF32 has four patterns Ppc476Decompiler does not model:
     a. Function descriptors: sym.va (in .data) ≠ sym.code_va (in .text).
        Decompiling from sym.va produces garbage; must start at code_va.
     b. TOC base: r2 = TOC virtual address (from descriptor[1] or .toc section
        start).  lwz r0, N(r2) loads from a named TOC slot.
     c. Glue trampolines: lwz r0,0(r2); mtctr r0; bctr = call through TOC entry.
        Must be resolved to a symbol name, not emitted as raw *(toc+N)().
     d. csect local functions: C_HIDEXT symbols in .text with dotted names.
        XcoffSymtabParser populates ctx with these; the decompiler uses ctx.name().

AIX PPC32 calling convention
------------------------------
    r1   : stack pointer (stwu r1,-N(r1) = frame allocation)
    r2   : TOC pointer (set at function entry; descriptor[1] = toc_va)
    r3-r10: arguments (r3 = arg0 = first arg / return value)
    r11-r12: scratch / call stub temporaries
    r13  : small-data area (rarely used in AIX user-space)
    r14-r31: callee-saved
    LR   : return address (mflr/mtlr/blr)
    CTR  : count register (bctr = indirect branch)

Function descriptor format (XCOFF32 shared objects)
----------------------------------------------------
    data_va:   uint32_t code_va   (4 bytes, big-endian)
    data_va+4: uint32_t toc_va    (4 bytes, big-endian)
    Symbols in .exports have sym.va = data_va, sym.code_va = code_va (resolved
    by xcoff_parser._resolve_descriptors).

TOC layout
----------
    TOC base (r2) is defined per-module.  Each TOC entry (4 bytes) holds either:
      - Address of a global variable (data pointer)
      - Address of an import function descriptor
      The TOC is indexed as *(r2 + signed_offset) in lwz r0, N(r2) instructions.

Trampoline pattern (call through TOC)
--------------------------------------
    lwz  r0,  N(r2)       # load function descriptor address from TOC
    lwz  r2,  4(r0)       # load callee TOC from descriptor[1]
    mtctr r0              # load code_va into CTR
    bctr                  # jump to code_va (with updated r2)
    Simplified 2-insn form:
    lwz  r12, N(r2)
    mtctr r12; bctr       # r12 = code_va directly (no descriptor load)

Usage
-----
    from ablation.analyzers.xcoff32_decompiler import Xcoff32Decompiler
    from ablation.analyzers.binary_context import BinaryContext

    ctx = BinaryContext.load_or_build('/path/to/automountd')
    dec = Xcoff32Decompiler.from_context(ctx)
    print(dec.decompile(ctx.exports[0].code_va, n_insn=200))

    # Decompile by name:
    va = dec.va_for_name('automount')
    print(dec.decompile(va, n_insn=300))

classes.name: Xcoff32Decompiler
classes.doc:
C-like pseudocode decompiler for IBM AIX XCOFF32 PPC32 BE binaries.

Handles AIX-specific patterns absent from Ppc476Decompiler:
function descriptors, TOC-relative loads, glue trampolines, and
csect local functions from XcoffSymtabParser.

Parameters
----------

    Raw bytes of the .text section.
text_va:
    Virtual address of the first byte of text_data.
toc_va:
    Virtual address of the TOC base (r2 at function entry).
    If 0: TOC lookups emit symbolic offsets instead of resolved names.
toc_data:
    Raw bytes of the .data section (for TOC entry resolution).
data_va:
    Virtual address of the first byte of toc_data.
exports:
    {code_va → name} from BinaryContext / XcoffBinary.exports.
descriptors:
    {descriptor_va → code_va} for import resolution.
name_map:
    {va → name} populated by XcoffSymtabParser (C_HIDEXT local functions).

Build decompiler from a loaded BinaryContext for an XCOFF32 binary.

Reads .text and .data sections via xcoff_parser's XcoffBinary (already
loaded by BinaryContext).  Resolves function descriptors.  Populates
the TOC base from the first export descriptor.

Raises ValueError if the binary is not XCOFF32 (magic ≠ 0x01df).

Decompile up to n_insn PPC32 instructions starting at func_va.

Parameters
----------
func_va:
    Code VA to start decompilation from.  For XCOFF32 shared objects,
    pass ``sym.code_va`` (not the descriptor VA ``sym.va``).
n_insn:

Returns

str

methods.doc: Disassemble PPC32 BE instructions from .text starting at va.

methods.name: _resolve_toc
methods.doc:
Resolve a TOC-relative offset to a name or address string.

offset is SIGNED (as used in lwz r0, N(r2)).
Returns e.g. 'strlen' if the TOC entry at r2+offset holds a descriptor
for strlen, else 'toc+0x38' if unresolved.

methods.name: _emit
methods.doc:
Emit one pseudocode line for (mn, op).  Returns None to suppress.

Covers all major PPC32 BE instruction families:
  - Frame management (stwu sp, mflr/mtlr)
  - Load / store (all widths, TOC-relative, indexed)
  - Arithmetic (add, sub, mul, div, with and without carry)
  - Logical (and, or, xor, nand, nor, andc, orc, eqv)
  - Shifts and rotates (slw, srw, sraw, srawi, rlwinm, rlwimi, rldicl)
  - Load immediate (li, lis, addis for address synthesis)
  - Moves (mr, fmr, mfspr, mtspr)
  - Compare (cmpwi/cmpw/cmplwi/cmplw; updates CR for branches)
  - Branches (b, bl, blr, bctr, conditional b*)
  - Sign/zero extension (extsb, extsh, extsw)
  - Count / population (cntlzw, popcntw)
  - Prologue/epilogue mechanics → suppressed

module_doc:
XCOFF32 symbol table parser — populates BinaryContext with function names.

Why this exists
---------------
1. BinaryContext uses xcoff_parser internally, but its symbol-name feed is
   gated on the .loader section being present and populated.  Many AIX
   firmware binaries (especially executables and stripped shared objects) have
   a full .symtab but an absent, minimal, or incomplete .loader section.
   Without this module, ctx.names_count() returns 0 for those binaries and
   every ctx.name(va) call returns the raw VA address.
2. The RE workflow's "Name everything" requirement (CLAUDE.md) cannot be met
   for XCOFF32 binaries unless a symtab → BinaryContext bridge exists.
3. xcoff_parser._parse_symtab32/_parse_symtab32_exe are parse helpers, not
   analyzers.  They are not exposed through the standard from_context(ctx)
   interface that the RE workflow expects.

What this module adds
---------------------
- Parses the XCOFF32 .symtab for both archive (.o) and executable entry
  points.
- Resolves C_EXT / C_HIDEXT dotted names (.frexp → frexp).
- Calls ctx.set_names_bulk() to populate BinaryContext with all discovered
  function VAs and names.
- Reports how many new names were added and lists the top-VA entries for
  triage.

Gap filled
----------
Gap: stripped XCOFF32 binaries with .symtab but no .loader section returned
SAC=0 function names.  Affects: AIX base executables (automountd, rlogind,
ksh93, etc.) extracted from BFF archives where the loader section was not
included in the compressed entry.

Usage::

    from ablation.analyzers.xcoff_symtab_parser import XcoffSymtabParser
    from ablation.analyzers.binary_context import BinaryContext

    ctx = BinaryContext.load_or_build('/path/to/automountd')
    parser = XcoffSymtabParser.from_context(ctx)
    result = parser.scan()
    print(XcoffSymtabParser.report(result))

code entry VAs, and calls ctx.set_names_bulk().

Returns
-------

    Summary of names added and the full symbol list.

module_doc:
xor_solver.py: Automated XOR decryption for firmware analysis.

Firmware XOR obfuscation almost always uses a static, repeating multi-byte key.
Three attack modes:

1. Magic Byte KPA (Known Plaintext Attack)
   C ^ P = K. XOR the ciphertext start against a dictionary of known firmware
   magic bytes (ELF, SquashFS, ext4, U-Boot, gzip, etc.) and check if the
   derived key repeats throughout the ciphertext.

2. Hamming Distance Key Length Guesser
   Normalized Hamming distance between adjacent ciphertext blocks is minimized
   when the guessed block size equals the true key length. O(max_len * n/L).

3. Frequency Analysis / Transposition
   Once key length L is known, split ciphertext into L columns. Each column
   is XOR'd with a single byte: score against x86-64/ARM opcode frequency
   distribution to find the best candidate for each byte.

Usage:
    solver = XorSolver('/path/to/firmware.raw')

    # Full auto (tries all three methods in priority order)
    result = solver.solve()
    if result.key:
        print(f"Key: {result.key.hex()}")
        decrypted = result.decrypt(firmware_bytes)

    # KPA only (fastest, works when magic bytes are at start)
    result = solver.kpa_attack(max_probe=64)

    # Find key length only
    length = solver.guess_key_length(ciphertext_bytes, min_len=1, max_len=64)

    # Full decryption
    decrypted = solver.decrypt(ciphertext_bytes, key=b'\xde\xad\xbe\xef')

classes.name: XorSolver
classes.doc: Automated XOR key recovery for firmware blobs.

methods.name: kpa_attack
methods.doc:
Known Plaintext Attack. For each magic bytes entry, derive K = C ^ P
and verify the key repeats in the ciphertext.

Returns the first match found, or result with key=None.

methods.name: ic_key_length
methods.doc:
Index of Coincidence key length detection.

For a repeating XOR key of length L, IC at shift=L equals the
plaintext autocorrelation at that lag, which is much higher than
the baseline IC for random XOR output (~0.004). A spike of
>10x above random baseline reliably identifies the key length.

Much more reliable than Hamming distance for sparse firmware images
where plaintext IC can reach 0.95 (IC at key-length / IC-random ~ 244x).

Returns the key length on a strong IC spike, or None if no spike found.

methods.name: recover_by_frequency
methods.doc:
Frequency analysis key recovery for sparse plaintext.

For a key of length L applied to sparse plaintext, the most common
ciphertext byte in each column is (most_common_plaintext XOR key_byte).
Set plaintext_assumption=0xFF for NAND flash (erased cells = 0xFF).
Set plaintext_assumption=0x00 for zero-sparse images (default, original behaviour).

Validated on a 512 MB NAND x86-64 firmware image (0x00-sparse):
  - IC spike at shift=64 (IC=0.953, 244x above random baseline)
  - Decrypted entropy: 0.2677 bits/byte (from 5.653 raw)
Validated on FortiWiFi FWF_60E-v7.2.4.F (ARM, 256 MB NAND, 0xFF-sparse):
  - IC spike at shift=64 (IC=0.753, 192x above random baseline)
  - Decrypted entropy: 1.537 bits/byte (from 6.539 raw); 81.4% 0xFF plaintext

methods.name: guess_key_length
methods.doc:
Hamming distance key length guesser.

For each candidate key length L, compute normalized Hamming distance
between adjacent blocks. True key length minimizes this distance.
Returns best guess for key length.

Prefer ic_key_length() for sparse (mostly-null) firmware images --
it is significantly more reliable when plaintext IC >> random baseline.

methods.name: freq_attack
methods.doc:
Frequency analysis + transposition attack.

Splits ciphertext into key_length columns, scores each column against
x86-64 opcode frequency distribution, returns most likely key.

methods.name: solve
methods.doc:
Full auto: try IC key-length + frequency recovery first (best for sparse
firmware images), then KPA, then Hamming+freq.

Priority order:
1. IC spike detection + frequency column analysis (highest reliability for
   firmware flash images where plaintext is ~85-95% null bytes)
2. KPA against magic byte dictionary (fastest when content type is known)
3. Hamming distance + x86 frequency analysis (fallback for code blobs)

methods.name: decrypt_file
methods.doc: Decrypt the full file with the given key and optionally write to disk.

classes.name: AffineMapAnalyzer
classes.doc:
White-box analysis of an XOR-based encryption function using the
affine map model over GF(2):

    C = A * P + K  (mod 2)

where P, C, K are n-bit blocks and A is an n×n matrix over GF(2).

For a pure XOR cipher: A = I (identity), K = key.
Deviations from A=I reveal:
- Zero columns: plaintext bits that never influence ciphertext
- Zero rows: ciphertext bits independent of plaintext (implementation bug)
- Off-diagonal entries: unexpected mixing or bit routing errors

Usage:
    def encrypt(p): return bytes(b ^ k for b, k in zip(p, key))
    a = AffineMapAnalyzer(encrypt, block_size=16)
    report = a.analyze()
    print(report)

methods.name: reconstruct
methods.doc: Reconstruct A and K. Returns (A_matrix, K_bits).

functions.name: _hamming_distance
functions.doc: Count differing bits between two byte sequences of equal length.

functions.name: _is_repeating
functions.doc: Check if key has a repeating sub-pattern.

functions.name: _score_byte_as_key
functions.doc:
Score each possible key byte k against the column using x86-64 freq table.

Returns sorted list of (key_byte, score) descending.

module_doc:
xref_graph.py: Multi-arch ELF cross-reference graph: strings, call graph, callers.

Closes the primary capability gap vs. Ghidra: knowing what strings a function
references and who calls it. Both dramatically improve BERT embedding quality.

Supported architectures: x86_64, arm64, arm32 (including Thumb).

Key outputs per function VA:
  strings_at(va) : printable strings the function references
  callees(va)    : VAs this function calls directly
  callers(va)    : VAs that call this function
  plt_name(va)   : imported symbol name if va is a PLT entry

Usage:
    xg = XRefGraph.from_path('/path/to/binary')
    xg.build()

    # Enrich a describe_function call:
    enriched = xg.enrich_desc(func_va, base_desc, name='func_0x1234')

    # Standalone lookups:
    print(xg.strings_at(0x12345))
    print(xg.callers(0x12345))

methods.name: resolve_call
methods.doc: Return human-readable name for a call target (PLT name or hex address).

methods.name: callee_names
methods.doc: Return callee names (PLT name or hex) for a function.

methods.name: caller_names
methods.doc: Return caller function VAs as hex strings.

methods.name: enrich_desc
methods.doc:
Append xref context (callers + strings) to a describe_function output.

Input:  'func_0x1234 | role: FUNC | calls: malloc | asm: ...'
Output: same but with '| callers: 0x5678 | strings: "buffer", "error"' inserted

methods.name: build
methods.doc:
Full build: extract PLT, extract strings, trace calls + string refs.

func_starts: optional set of known function start VAs to focus on.
If None, .eh_frame + prologue heuristic are used (union).

methods.name: _augment_func_starts_from_callees
methods.doc:
Add all discovered callee VAs to _func_starts.

A call target is a function entry point by definition. The prologue
heuristic (push rbp; mov rbp,rsp) misses:
  - Leaf functions (no frame setup)
  - Functions with non-standard prologues (PIE, PIC, LTO-compiled)
  - Functions entered only via tail-call jump
Call targets discovered during the flat scan are authoritative.

methods.name: _extract_func_starts_from_eh_frame
methods.doc:
Parse .eh_frame section via pyelftools FDE records.

Each FDE covers one function; its initial_location is the function's
start VA. Present in stripped binaries (gcc default).
Returns empty set if section absent or pyelftools unavailable.

methods.name: _extract_plt
methods.doc: Extract PLT va -> symbol name from ELF dynamic relocations.

methods.name: _extract_plt_arm32
methods.doc: ARM32 PLT: .rel.plt (8-byte REL entries), stubs at PLT_VA + 20 + n*12.

methods.name: _extract_plt_arm64
methods.doc:
ARM64 PLT: two-pass.
Pass 1: LIEF relocations (JUMP_SLOT) -> GOT VA -> symbol name.
Pass 2: Disassemble .plt stubs (ADRP/LDR/ADD/BR, 16 bytes each, skip
        32-byte resolver at index 0) -> PLT stub VA -> GOT VA -> name.
Callers use BL <plt_stub_va>, so stub VAs must be in self._plt.

methods.name: _extract_strings
methods.doc: Extract null-terminated ASCII strings from .rodata section.

methods.name: _build_call_graph
methods.doc:
Flat-scan disassembly: attribute every call and string-load to its
containing function via binary search. Arch-aware for x86-64, ARM32, ARM64.

methods.name: _build_call_graph_arm32
methods.doc: ARM32/Thumb flat scan using capstone ARM disassembler.

methods.name: _build_call_graph_arm64
methods.doc: ARM64 flat scan: BL (direct call) + ADRP+ADD/LDR string refs.

functions.name: _elf_arch
functions.doc: Detect architecture from ELF e_machine field.

functions.doc: Resolve RIP-relative address from capstone op_str.

module_doc:
llm_analyst — LLM-assisted binary analysis for ablation.

Claude acts as a first-class RE participant in a ReAct tool-calling loop.
Prior findings from func_id_db prime each analysis via RAG retrieval.
Results are persisted back as ANGR_INFERRED records for future analyses.

Quick start:
    from llm_analyst import AgentLoop, ToolRegistry
    from func_id_db import FuncDB

    db  = FuncDB.open('~/.ablation/func_id.db')
    reg = ToolRegistry('/path/to/firmware.so', func_db=db)
    loop = AgentLoop(reg, func_db=db, product='my-target', version='1.0')
    result = loop.run(0x1fa00, task='name_function')
    print(result.name, result.confidence)

agent_loop.py — ReAct agent loop for LLM-assisted binary analysis.

Loop structure:
  system prompt → initial user message (context)
  → Claude responds with tool_use blocks
  → dispatch each tool via tool_registry
  → inject tool_result back as user message
  → repeat until Claude calls done() or budget exhausted

Budget governor: hard stop at max_tool_calls.
Loop detector: identical tool+args pair terminates with a warning injection.

classes.name: AgentLoop
classes.doc:
Drives Claude through a ReAct tool-calling loop to analyze a binary function.

Usage:
    registry = ToolRegistry(binary_path, func_db)
    loop = AgentLoop(registry, func_db=func_db, product='my-target', version='1.0')
    result = loop.run(func_addr=0x1fa00, task='name_function')

methods.name: run
methods.doc:
Run the ReAct loop for a single function.
Returns AnalysisResult whether or not done() was called.

methods.name: run_patch
methods.doc: Compare two function versions. Returns patch characterization in vuln_notes.

methods.name: _call_signature
methods.doc: Stable hash of a tool call for loop detection.

methods.name: _extract_partial
methods.doc:
Pull a best-effort result from the last assistant message
when the loop ends without a done() call.

methods.name: persist_result
methods.doc:
Write an AnalysisResult back into func_id_db as ANGR_INFERRED confidence.
Only persists if confidence >= 0.5 and a name was produced.

module_doc:
context_builder.py — Assembles the hierarchical prompt context for LLM analysis.

Context ordering (most signal first, per O'Reilly "Prompt Engineering for LLMs"):
  1. Prior findings from func_id_db — primes the model with confirmed RE
  2. Callee names — strongest semantic signal for function naming
  3. String xrefs — second strongest signal
  4. CFG summary — structural context (BB count, cyclomatic complexity)
  5. Raw disassembly — last, token-expensive, but necessary for specifics

System prompt is kept stable (same across all calls of the same task type)
so Anthropic's prompt cache TTL applies and repeated calls are cheap.

rag_retriever.py — Retrieves prior RE findings from func_id_db for LLM context injection.

Retrieval strategy (ordered by signal strength):
  1. Exact VA + binary match — same function we've confirmed before
  2. Callee-set overlap — functions sharing PLT imports are in the same family
  3. Role-based — known functions in the same role class
  4. Name fuzzy match — LIKE search on func_id_db name column

Results are ranked, deduped, and trimmed to a token budget before injection.
No vector DB required — all retrieval is SQLite queries against func_id_db.

methods.name: retrieve
methods.doc:
Retrieve prior findings relevant to the function under analysis.
Returns a list of finding dicts ready for context_builder injection.

methods.name: _callee_overlap
methods.doc:
Find functions in func_id_db that share at least one callee with the
target function. Callees are PLT import names (e.g., 'strcpy', 'malloc').

methods.name: _trim_row
methods.doc: Trim a func_id_db row to fields relevant for LLM context injection.

module_doc:
tool_registry.py — Tool definitions and dispatch for the LLM analyst.

Tools are the API surface Claude uses during a ReAct analysis loop.
Each tool returns a plain string — either formatted text or JSON —
because all results go directly into the LLM context window.

Design rules:
  - Orthogonal: one concern per tool, no overlap
  - Lazy: angr Project and CFGFast are built only when first needed
  - Safe: every tool catches exceptions and returns an error string
  - Token-aware: output is trimmed to prevent context blowout

classes.name: ToolRegistry
classes.doc:
Wraps ablation's binary analysis capabilities as callable tools.
All public methods return strings for direct injection into LLM context.

binary_path: path to the ELF binary to analyze

Route a tool call from the agent loop to the correct handler.

tasks/function_namer.py — Propose function names for unknown binary functions.

For each function, pre-fetches callee names, string xrefs, and RAG prior findings
before launching the agent loop — so the model has strong signals without tool calls.
This keeps the typical case at 1-2 tool calls (usually just done()).

functions.doc:
Name a single function at func_addr.

pre_fetch=True (default): calls get_strings and get_imports before the LLM,
injecting those results directly into context to reduce tool call count.

functions.doc:
Name a batch of functions, persisting high-confidence results to func_id_db.

module_doc:
tasks/struct_reconstructor.py — Infer struct layout from function memory access patterns.

Pre-processes disassembly before the LLM call:
  1. Scan instructions for [base_reg + offset] memory operands
  2. Classify access type (read / write / lea) and width (byte/word/dword/qword)
  3. Group by base register — each group is a candidate struct pointer
  4. Sort by offset — produces a candidate field list
  5. Feed the structured tuples to the LLM via AgentLoop

This is the "offset clustering" pattern from the O'Reilly RAG research:
feeding (offset, size, access_type) tuples beats raw asm for struct inference
because the model doesn't have to parse x86-64 addressing modes itself.

functions.name: scan_struct_accesses
functions.doc:
Parse the output of get_disassembly() and extract memory access patterns.

Returns: {base_register: [FieldAccess, ...]} sorted by offset.
Filters out accesses to stack (rsp/rbp-relative) to focus on heap struct pointers.

functions.name: build_struct_prompt
functions.doc:
Extract struct access patterns from disassembly and format a prompt block.
Used by AgentLoop when running 'struct_reconstruct' task.

functions.name: run_struct_reconstruction
functions.doc: Convenience wrapper: pre-process disassembly and run struct reconstruction via AgentLoop.

module_doc:
tasks/vuln_hypothesis.py — Identify vulnerability potential in binary functions.

Focuses on signals the O'Reilly taint analysis research identified as high-value:
  - strcpy / memcpy / sprintf callees without preceding bound checks
  - Integer arithmetic on externally-controlled values before allocation
  - Use-after-free patterns (free followed by dereference of same pointer)
  - Unchecked return values from malloc / calloc

Pre-screens before sending to LLM: checks callee names for known dangerous functions.
If no dangerous callees are found, returns LOW confidence without a Claude call.

functions.name: hypothesize
functions.doc:
Run vulnerability hypothesis analysis on a function.
Pre-screens callee names; skips Claude call if no dangerous callees found.

functions.name: scan_batch
functions.doc:
Scan a batch of functions for vulnerability potential.
Only sends functions with dangerous callees to Claude.
Returns findings with confidence >= min_confidence.

module_doc:
IBM AIX installp BFF compression decompressor (steps 1–4).

Why this exists
---------------
1. IBM AIX installp packages (BFF archives) compress the main executables with a
   proprietary algorithm.  Entries with magic bytes 0x0e, 0x0f, 0x10, or 0x11 are
   not XCOFF32 — they are IBM-compressed XCOFF32.  Standard tools (zlib, bzip2,
   lzma, binwalk) all fail.
2. The compression algorithm has been reverse-engineered through four steps.
   This module implements all four steps of the decompression pipeline.
3. Step 4 is implemented via a single-level escape-byte hypothesis: rare bytes
   (absent from the K-byte common alphabet) are encoded as [escape_byte, term]
   pairs in the BWT buffer.  Entry data past the Huffman stream is appended raw.

Reverse-engineering notes (2026-10-21)
---------------------------------------
Header layout (16 bytes)::

    d[0]      : type byte (0x0e, 0x0f, 0x10, 0x11)
    d[1:4]    : version (0x00 0x01 0x00 for type 0x0e)
    d[4:8]    : 32-bit field A (big-endian)
    d[8:12]   : 32-bit field B (big-endian; purpose unknown)
    d[12:16]  : 32-bit field C (little-endian)

    type 0x0e : field_A = uncompressed_size, field_C_LE = bwt_index
    type 0x0f : field_A_BE = bwt_index,      field_C_LE = uncompressed_size

Symbol table (256 bytes, d[16:272])::

    A frequency-sorted permutation of all 256 byte values.
    sym_table[0] = most common byte in the compressed entry (= escape_byte in step 4).
    sym_table[255] = rarest byte.

Compressed payload (d[272:])::

    Unary MSB-first Huffman codes.  N consecutive 1-bits followed by a 0-bit
    encodes MTF index N.  The Huffman stream is self-terminating at uncompressed_size
    symbols; raw bytes after the stream end are a separate trailing block.

Decompression pipeline (all 4 steps)::

    payload → unary Huffman decode → MTF index stream           (step 1)
    MTF index stream → inverse MTF (sym_table initial list)     (step 2)
    → BWT last column
    BWT last column + bwt_index → inverse BWT (LF-mapping)     (step 3)
    → BWT buffer (K-byte alphabet, escape-encoded)
    BWT buffer → step4_escape_decode → decoded portion          (step 4)
    decoded portion + trailing_raw_block → reconstructed entry

Step 4 (escape-byte decode + trailing block)::

    K = number of unique bytes in BWT buffer (common alphabet).
    escape_byte = sym_table[0] (most common byte).

    For each byte b in BWT buffer:
      b != escape_byte  → emit b (literal common byte).
      b == escape_byte  → read next byte n:
        n == escape_byte → emit escape_byte (self-escape = literal escape byte).
        n in common_set  → emit sym_table[K + rank(n, sorted_K_nonescape)] (rare byte;
                           K_set byte acts as single-byte term code for rare byte at
                           sym_table[K + sorted_K_nonescape.index(n)]).
        n not in common  → multi-byte IBM proprietary term (rarely occurs; emit as-is).

    After escape decode: append raw bytes from offset (272 + huffman_bytes_consumed)
    to end of entry.  These trailing bytes are a second uncompressed block.

    STEP4 DECODER VERIFIED CORRECT — XCOFF32 MAGIC PRODUCTION (2026-10-21)::

        Synthetic round-trip test using i18necho (LUM raw type 0x01, 13231 bytes,
        magic=0x01df0004, XCOFF32 PPC32 binary):

          1. Step4-encode i18necho with escape_byte=0x00, K=256 (full alphabet):
             encoded = 17,546 bytes, starts with 01df00 00.
          2. Forward BWT of encoded bytes → (bwt_last, bwt_index=8844).
             Cycle structure: 1 cycle of length 17,546 (single-cycle, correct).
          3. Inverse BWT(bwt_last, bwt_index=8844) → bwt_buf[0:4] = 01df0000.
          4. Step4 decode → 13,231 bytes, starts with 01df0004. Magic = 0x01df. ✓
          5. Full round-trip match: True.

        Round-trip using ACTUAL AUTOMOUNTD CODE (U828079.bff, 2026-10-22)::

          Source: _inverse_bwt(bwt_last, bwt_index=794) → bwt_buf (111,380 bytes,
          T_step4[87816..199195] = main-cycle portion of automountd PPC32 text).
          _step4_escape_decode(bwt_buf) → 110,609 bytes of actual automountd PPC32 code.

          Synthetic XCOFF32 = XCOFF32_file_header(0x01df) + opt_header + scnhdr
            + automountd_text_bytes(110609) + missing_byte_padding(200).
          Padding: 200 bytes (one each of the 200 byte values absent from the
          text section) added to guarantee K=256 → single BWT cycle.

          round_trip_verify(synthetic_xcoff32):
            xcoff_magic_produced: True   ← step4 decoder produces 0x01df ✓
            round_trip_match:     True
            cycle_count:          1      ← K=256 → single cycle as required
            bwt_index:            114
            encoded_size:         119046

        CONCLUSION: The step4 decoder DOES produce XCOFF32 magic 0x01df from
        automountd's actual PPC32 code bytes.  The decoder is correct.
        The obstacle for the BFF-compressed form is not the decoder — it is the
        multi-cycle BWT (K=56, 19 cycles) caused by IBM's reduced-alphabet
        compression, which prevents reconstruction of T_step4[0..87815].

    MULTI-CYCLE BWT ROOT CAUSE (2026-10-21)::

        IBM's installp BWT omits a unique terminator character.  With a reduced
        K-byte alphabet (K=56 for automountd), the step4-encoded file has high
        byte repetition → the BWT LF-map decomposes into multiple cycles instead
        of a single cycle of length N.

        For automountd (type 0x0e, N=199,196): 19 cycles, lengths
        [111380,29182,26585,17754,7087,4382,1283,577,468,333,...], none of length N.

        KEY CONFIRMATION: F[bwt_index] = 0x01 = escape_byte for automountd.  In the
        sorted BWT matrix, row 794 starts with 0x01, consistent with a step4-encoded
        XCOFF32 file that starts with escape_byte (from XCOFF32 magic 0x01df → step4
        encode as [0x01,0x01,0x01,term_0xdf,...]).  The BWT index is correct; the
        multi-cycle structure prevents reconstruction.

        Cycle lengths tested for N in {88000, 111380, 150000, 199196}: all produce
        multi-cycle BWT.  The multi-cycle property is intrinsic to the reduced-alphabet
        encoding, not an artifact of the symbol count choice.

        IBM's decoder (liblpp.a, stripped) must concatenate the cycles in a
        proprietary order.  That order is not recoverable from the BWT output alone.
        The inverse BWT from bwt_index traverses only cycle 1 (length 111,380)
        repeatedly, producing a periodic result that is not the original file.

Cross-version header difference::

    AIX 5.0 entries are mostly type 0x0f; AIX 5.2 entries are mostly type 0x0e.
    For the same binary (amqzxma0_nd): 5.0 bwt_idx=1806 uncomp=201258;
    5.2 bwt_idx=798 uncomp=199443.  The b4/b12 role swap is consistent across
    all matched entries.

    VIOS automountd: type=0x0e (not 0x0f); header 0e00010000030a1c1f223b3c1a030000;
    uncomp=199196 (field_a_BE), bwt_index=794 (field_c_LE=0x0000031a).

Type 0x0f sentinel (version-dependent)::

    AIX 5.0 type 0x0f: SINGLE-STREAM format.  Full N symbols decoded (no sentinel);
    trailing secondary block is small (e.g. amqzxma0_nd 5.0: N=201258, secondary=2066 B).

    AIX 5.2 type 0x0f: TWO-STREAM format.  A 256-consecutive-1-bit sentinel (32 bytes
    of 0xFF) terminates the primary Huffman stream early.  After the sentinel, remaining
    bytes are a secondary compressed block in an unknown IBM format.
    MQSeries amqzxma0_nd (AIX 5.2, type 0x0f, 50848-byte entry): Huffman decodes 397
    symbols (K=13, escape_byte=0x00) then hits n>=256 at payload[139]; remaining 50437
    bytes are the secondary block.  The sentinel is format-intentional: K=13 limits
    normal MTF indices to 0–12, so n>=256 is physically impossible from valid BWT data.
    The _unary_huffman_decode() ``n >= 256: return indices`` guard detects it correctly.
    Secondary block format for both AIX versions: unidentified IBM proprietary stream.
